nodes.title: Integral Witt comparison
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, compare quadratic forms q on finite projective modules, required to have perfect polar pairing b_q(x,y)=q(x+y)−q(x)−q(y), with perfect symmetric bilinear forms. Polarisation induces σ:Wq(R)→Ws(R). These are metabolic quotients, with a direct-summand Lagrangian and, on the quadratic side, q vanishing on it. For 2 invertible σ is an isomorphism; its inverse sends b to x↦b(x,x)/2. Identify degree zero of periodic Lq and Ls with these classical Witt groups, using the supplier’s surgery comparison.
hypotheses: R commutative; modules finite projective; perfect means the adjoint to the R-dual is an isomorphism.
proofSteps: Import symmetric spaces and the exact Witt quotient from GN.6, and request the quadratic carrier and degree-zero comparison under gap G1.
Polarisation respects isometries, orthogonal sums and metabolic forms. When 2 is a unit, the half-diagonal is inverse by the quadratic identity.
Use actual Mathlib QuadraticMap and its polarBilin; do not treat nonzero determinant as unimodularity over a ring.

nodes.title: Integral Witt injection
nodes.statement: For a Dedekind domain R with fraction field K, Ws(R)→Ws(K) is injective. If char K≠2, Wq(R)→Wq(K) and σ:Wq(R)→Ws(R) are injective. If char R=2, σ is zero: every polar form is alternating and every nonsingular alternating form over a Dedekind domain is metabolic.
hypotheses: R Dedekind domain; finite projective nonsingular forms; no perfection assumption on K in characteristic 2.
proofSteps: A generic Lagrangian L_K descends to the saturated intersection P∩L_K. The quotient is torsion-free, hence projective over R, and the rank-half saturated isotropic submodule equals its perpendicular by perfection. This gives a direct-summand Lagrangian.
For a quadratic form use the same argument and q=0 over K on the Lagrangian. Equivalently in characteristic not 2, b(x,x)=2q(x)=0 and R is 2-torsion-free.

In characteristic 2 the polar is alternating; split symplectic projective summands by choosing a line summand and the perfect pairing. This concerns bilinear metabolicity, not vanishing of quadratic Arf invariants.

nodes.title: Second residue
nodes.statement: For each nonzero prime p of a Dedekind domain R, construct the symmetric Witt boundary ∂p:Ws(K)→Ws(kp;lp), where lp=p⁻¹/R at p is the canonical residue duality line. Choose a uniformizer π only to identify lp with kp. In that coordinate ∂p⟨πu⟩=⟨ū⟩ and ∂p⟨u⟩=0 for units u; valuation parity determines the general rank-one value. The family has finite support and gives ∂0:Ws(K)→⊕p Ws(kp;lp).
hypotheses: R Dedekind; residue characteristic and fraction characteristic may be 2; the rank-one formula concerns symmetric bilinear forms.
proofSteps: Import the residue coefficient line from GN.6 and request its L-theory localization form (R1).
Compute the boundary using the torsion linking pairing on the dual lattice modulo the integral lattice, identifying the coefficient by multiplication by π.
Diagonalize nonalternating summands over K; alternating summands are metabolic. Only finitely many primes divide denominators and the Gram determinant. Track the line when the uniformizer changes.

nodes.statement: For k=F_(2^r), r≥1, and a finite-dimensional quadratic map q with perfect polar form, define Arf_k(q) as Tr_(k/F2)(Σ_i q(e_i)q(f_i)) in F2 for a symplectic basis (e_i,f_i). A binary plane ax²+xy+by² is hyperbolic precisely when Tr(ab)=0; solve the associated Artin–Schreier equation. Pair two trace-one planes to obtain a hyperbolic form.
Under scalar extension use Tr_(k′/F2)(a)=m Tr_(k/F2)(a) for a in k. This is essential for the Eisenstein computation.

nodes.title: Symmetric Dedekind table

In particular there is an exact sequence 0→Ls_(2a)(R)→Ls_(2a)(K)→⊕p Ls_(2a)(kp)→Ls_(2a−1)(R)→0.

Use the field L table and degree-zero injectivity to break the localization long exact sequence into the displayed short pieces.

nodes.title: Arithmetic fracture
nodes.statement: Let R be a ring, M an invertible module with involution over R, in the coefficient-duality sense of the source, and ℓ a positive integer. Assume ordinary ℓ-adic completion R̂_ℓ represents derived completion (bounded ℓ-power torsion suffices). For each m∈Z∪{±∞}, the square Dp(R)→Dp(R̂_ℓ), over Dc(R[1/ℓ])→Dc′(R̂_ℓ[1/ℓ]), with structures Q_M^(≥m), is Poincaré–Verdier. Here c and c′ are precisely the involution-stable images of the respective K0 maps. Applying GW or L gives a homotopy pullback square.

proofSteps: The underlying perfect-complex square follows from the derived localization/completion pullback. Import this general categorical input under G1.

Apply the Poincaré–Verdier criterion [II] Proposition 4.5.5; the Tate obstruction vanishes on the rational overlap. Then use localizing invariance of GW and L.

nodes.title: Quadratic isometry lifting
nodes.statement: If R is complete and separated for powers of an involution-stable two-sided ideal J, projectives and nonsingular quadratic forms lift from R/J. Two nonsingular quadratic refinements on the same finite projective module which are isometric modulo J are isometric over R by an isometry reducing to the prescribed one. No invertibility of 2 is assumed.
hypotheses: Involution and quadratic form parameter compatible with J; complete and separated, not merely dense; finite projective modules.
proofSteps: Lift idempotents and homomorphisms of projectives. Use Nakayama to recognize a lifted polar map as invertible.
Lift the prescribed residue isometry first as a module map. Apply successive quadratic corrections: error in J^r is replaced by error in J^(2r).

Completeness gives the convergent product of the corrections and separation turns the limiting equality into equality. This is the quadratic lifting theorem; the analogous arbitrary symmetric statement at 2 is false.

nodes.title: Dyadic parity obstruction
nodes.statement: For R as in the preceding theorem and d≥2, rank parity induces a canonical surjection A(R)→(Z/2)^d/Δ(Z/2)≃(Z/2)^(d−1). Hence A(R) is nonzero. For d=1 the same quotient is zero and gives no vanishing conclusion about A.

nodes.statement: The map Wq(Z_2)→Wq(O) is zero, since its residue degree is 2. Let t be the image in Ws(O) of the Arf-one form q=x²+xy+ζy² over O. It has order 2 and signed determinant d=1−4ζ. Norm_(E/Q2)(d)=21 is not a Q2 square. Consequently t∉⟨u⟩⊂Ws(O): the only possible nonzero order-two class there is 2u, whose signed determinant −1 has square norm. Thus ⟨u⟩∩⟨t⟩=0.

Compute (1−4ζ)(1−4ζ²)=21. A Q2 unit is square only if congruent to 1 mod 8, whereas 21≡5. The signed determinant in the even-dimensional Witt ideal is multiplicative under orthogonal sum, so comparison with 0 and 2u proves the intersection claim.
